blocks.text: 1. Token Budgeting

blocks.alt: A total token budget splits into fixed components and remaining space for chunks

blocks.text: Token Budgeting, opening the Context Management module by treating context space as a finite resource, shifts focus from selecting chunks to fitting them into an actual prompt.
It allocates a fixed number of tokens across every piece competing for space in the prompt.
2. Re-Ranking Recap
Eight topics covered ordering and selecting the best possible chunks.
Context management covers how those selected chunks actually fit into a real prompt.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Module","Role"],"rows":[["Re-Ranking","Orders and selects the best candidate chunks"],["Context Management","Fits those chunks into an actual prompt"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Every Part Of The Prompt Takes Space

blocks.alt: System prompt, retrieved chunks, and query all consume tokens

blocks.text: In Deep Learning Fundamentals, system instructions, chat history, and retrieved chunks all compete for the same limited space.
Retrieved context is only one of several consumers of that shared budget.
4. Counting Tokens, Not Characters

blocks.alt: Character count is compared against token count

blocks.text: In Deep Learning Fundamentals, a model's context limit is measured in tokens, not characters or words.
Budgeting accurately requires counting with the actual tokenizer, not a rough estimate.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A rough estimate like four characters per token can drift noticeably from the actual tokenizer count, especially for text with unusual punctuation, code, or non English characters, risking a budget overrun.

blocks.text: 5. Reserving Space For Fixed Components

blocks.alt: The total budget reserves space for the system prompt and query

blocks.text: System instructions and conversation history need their space reserved before anything else.
Only the remaining space after those fixed costs becomes available for retrieved context.
6. Allocating The Remainder Across Chunks

blocks.alt: The remaining budget divides among selected chunks

blocks.text: As with the last decision before the model in Top-K Selection, the remaining token budget determines how many retrieved chunks can actually fit.
A larger fixed overhead leaves less room for retrieved content.
7. Reserving Output Space Too

blocks.alt: An input budget reserves output space

blocks.text: The model's response itself also consumes tokens from that same total limit.
Forgetting to reserve output space can leave the model unable to finish its answer.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Filling the entire context limit with input and leaving no room for output, causes a response to get cut off mid sentence, since the model has no remaining token budget left to complete it.

blocks.text: 8. Dynamic Budgeting Across Queries
Different queries naturally need different amounts of retrieved context.
A fixed budget for every query wastes space on simple questions and starves complex ones.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When Careful Token Budgeting Matters Most

blocks.alt: A tight context window points toward budgeting tokens carefully

blocks.text: Systems with long conversation history or many components need careful budgeting.
Simple, single turn queries with generous context limits rarely hit the budget ceiling at all.
10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates allocating a token budget across fixed components, retrieved chunks, and reserved output space.

code.content:
total_context_limit = 8000
system_instructions_tokens = 300
conversation_history_tokens = 1200
reserved_output_tokens = 1500

def calculate_available_for_retrieval(total_limit, fixed_costs, output_reserve):
    # reserving space for fixed components
    return total_limit - sum(fixed_costs) - output_reserve

fixed_costs = [system_instructions_tokens, conversation_history_tokens]
available_for_chunks = calculate_available_for_retrieval(total_context_limit, fixed_costs, reserved_output_tokens)

print(f"Total context limit: {total_context_limit} tokens")
print(f"Fixed costs (reserving space for fixed components): {sum(fixed_costs)} tokens")
print(f"Reserved output space (reserving output space too): {reserved_output_tokens} tokens")
print(f"Available for retrieved chunks: {available_for_chunks} tokens")

average_chunk_tokens = 250
max_chunks_that_fit = available_for_chunks // average_chunk_tokens
print(f"\nApproximate chunks that fit (allocating the remainder across chunks): {max_chunks_that_fit}")

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Running this example shows the available budget for retrieved chunks shrinking once fixed costs and reserved output space are subtracted.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Estimating token count roughly from character count instead of using the actual tokenizer.
Forgetting to reserve space for the model's own output, risking a cut off response.
Applying the same fixed budget to every query regardless of its actual complexity.
Filling the entire available budget with retrieved chunks without accounting for fixed overhead.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Token budgeting allocates a fixed number of tokens across every piece competing for prompt space.
System instructions, conversation history, and retrieved chunks all compete for the same limited space.
A model's context limit is measured in tokens, requiring the actual tokenizer for accurate counting.
Fixed components need their space reserved before anything else, leaving the remainder for retrieval.
The remaining token budget determines how many retrieved chunks can actually fit.
The model's own response consumes tokens too, requiring reserved output space.
Different queries naturally need different amounts of context, favoring dynamic budgeting.
A fixed budget for every query wastes space on simple ones and can starve complex ones.
